{{short description|Formulas about vectors in three-dimensional Euclidean space}}
The following are important identities in [[Vector space|vector algebra]]. Identities that only involve the magnitude of a vector <math>\|\mathbf A\|</math> and the [[dot product]] (scalar product) of two vectors '''A'''·'''B''', apply to vectors in any dimension, while identities that use the [[cross product]] (vector product) '''A'''×'''B''' only apply in three dimensions, since the cross product is only defined there.{{refn|group=nb|There is also a [[seven-dimensional cross product]] of vectors that relates to multiplication in the [[octonion]]s, but it does not satisfy these three-dimensional identities.}}<ref name=Albright>{{cite book |title=Albright's chemical engineering handbook |author=Lyle Frederick Albright |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HYB3Udjx_FYC&pg=PA68 |page=68 |isbn=978-0-8247-5362-7 |publisher=CRC Press |chapter=§2.5.1 Vector algebra |year=2008}}</ref>
Most of these relations can be dated to founder of vector calculus [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]], if not earlier.<ref name=autogenerated2 />

==Magnitudes==

The magnitude of a vector '''A''' can be expressed using the dot product:

:<math>\|\mathbf A \|^2 = \mathbf {A \cdot A} </math>

In three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], the magnitude of a vector is determined from its three components using [[Pythagoras' theorem]]:

:<math>\|\mathbf A \|^2 = A_1^2 + A_2^2 +A_3^2 </math>

==Inequalities==

*The [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]]: <math>\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} \le \left\|\mathbf A \right\| \left\|\mathbf B \right\| </math>
*The [[triangle inequality]]: <math>\|\mathbf{A + B}\| \le \| \mathbf{A}\| + \|\mathbf{B}\| </math>
*The [[Triangle_inequality#Reverse_triangle_inequality |reverse triangle inequality]]: <math>\|\mathbf{A - B}\| \ge \Bigl| \| \mathbf{A}\| - \|\mathbf{B}\| \Bigr| </math>

==Angles==

The vector product and the scalar product of two vectors define the angle between them, say ''θ'':<ref name=Albright/><ref name=Hildebrand>

{{cite book |title=Methods of applied mathematics |author=Francis Begnaud Hildebrand |page=24 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=17EZkWPz_eQC&pg=PA24|isbn=0-486-67002-3 |edition=Reprint of Prentice-Hall 1965 2nd|publisher=Courier Dover Publications |year=1992}}
</ref>

:<math>\sin \theta =\frac{\|\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}\|}{\left\|\mathbf A \right\| \left\|\mathbf B \right\|} \quad ( -\pi < \theta \le \pi ) </math>
To satisfy the [[right-hand rule]], for positive ''θ'', vector '''B''' is counter-clockwise from '''A''', and for negative ''θ'' it is clockwise.
:<math>\cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{\left\|\mathbf A \right\| \left\|\mathbf B \right\|} \quad ( -\pi < \theta \le \pi )</math>

The [[Pythagorean trigonometric identity]] then provides:

:<math>  \left\|\mathbf{A \times B}\right\|^2 +(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B})^2 = \left\|\mathbf A \right\|^2  \left\|\mathbf B \right\|^2 </math>

(This may also be seen by identifying a vector <math>\mathbf{V}=V_x \mathbf{i}+V_y \mathbf{j}+V_z \mathbf{k}</math> with the corresponding imaginary [[quaternion]], so that  the quaternion product is <math>\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} = -\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}\,+\,\mathbf{A}{\times}\mathbf{B}</math> ; then the above identity follows from the multiplicative property <math>\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\| = \|\mathbf{A}\|\,\|\mathbf{B}\|</math>.)

If a vector '''A''' = (''A<sub>x</sub>, A<sub>y</sub>, A<sub>z</sub>'') makes angles ''α'', ''β'', ''γ'' with an orthogonal set of ''x-'', ''y-'' and ''z-''axes, then:

:<math> \cos \alpha = \frac{ A_x }{ \sqrt {A_x^2 +A_y^2 +A_z^2} }  = \frac {A_x} {\| \mathbf A \|} \ , </math>
and analogously for angles β, γ. Consequently:
:<math>\mathbf A = \left\|\mathbf A \right\|\left( \cos (\alpha) \,  \mathbf  i  
+  \cos (\beta)\,  \mathbf  j +  \cos (\gamma) \, \mathbf  k  \right) , </math>
where <math>\mathbf  i,  \mathbf  j, \mathbf  k</math> are the coordinate unit vectors.

==Areas and volumes==

The area Σ of a [[parallelogram]] with sides ''A'' and ''B'' containing the angle ''θ'' is:
:<math> \Sigma = AB \sin \theta , </math>
which will be recognized as the magnitude of the vector cross product of the vectors '''A''' and '''B''' lying along the sides of the parallelogram. That is:
:<math>\Sigma = \left\|\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B} \right\| = \sqrt{ \left\|\mathbf A\right\|^2 \left\|\mathbf B\right\|^2 - \left(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} \right)^2} \ . </math>

(If '''A''', '''B''' are two-dimensional vectors, this is equal to the determinant of the 2 × 2 matrix with rows '''A''', '''B'''.) The square of this expression is:<ref name=Courant>{{cite book |title=Introduction to calculus and analysis, Volume II |author=Richard Courant, Fritz John |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ngkQxS4eicgC&pg=PA191 |pages=190–195 |chapter=Areas of parallelograms and volumes of parallelepipeds in higher dimensions  |isbn=3-540-66569-2 |year=2000 |publisher=Springer |edition=Reprint of original 1974 Interscience}}</ref>
:<math>\Sigma^2 = (\mathbf{A \cdot A })(\mathbf{B \cdot B })-(\mathbf{A \cdot B })(\mathbf{B \cdot A })=\Gamma(\mathbf A,\ \mathbf B ) \ , </math>
where Γ('''A''', '''B''') is the [[Gram determinant]] of '''A''' and '''B''' defined by:

:<math>\Gamma(\mathbf A,\ \mathbf B )=\begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{A\cdot A} & \mathbf{A\cdot B} \\
 \mathbf{B\cdot A} & \mathbf{B\cdot B}  \end{vmatrix} \ . </math>

In a similar fashion, the squared volume ''V'' of a [[parallelepiped]] spanned by the three vectors '''A''', '''B''', '''C''' is given by the Gram determinant of the three vectors:<ref name=Courant/>
:<math>V^2 =\Gamma ( \mathbf A ,\ \mathbf B ,\  \mathbf C ) = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{A\cdot A} & \mathbf{A\cdot B} & \mathbf{A\cdot C} \\\mathbf{B\cdot A} & \mathbf{B\cdot B} & \mathbf{B\cdot C}\\
 \mathbf{C\cdot A} & \mathbf{C\cdot B} & \mathbf{C\cdot C}  \end{vmatrix} 
\ , </math>

Since '''A''', '''B, C''' are three-dimensional vectors, this is equal to the square of the [[scalar triple product]] <math>\det[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}] = |\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}|</math> below.

This process can be extended to ''n''-dimensions. Indeed, letting <math>M=\left[\begin{smallmatrix} \mathbf{A}_1\\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{A}_n\end{smallmatrix}\right]</math> be the <math>n\times n</math> matrix whose rows are the vectors <math>\mathbf{A}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{A}_n</math>, the Gram matrix <math>G</math> is product of <math>M</math> with its transpose, <math>\Gamma = M M^T</math>, so that <math>\Gamma =\det G = (\det M)^2 = V^2</math>.

==Addition and multiplication of vectors==

* [[Commutativity]] of addition: <math>\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{A}</math>.
* Commutativity of scalar product: <math>\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}</math>.
* [[Anticommutativity]] of cross product: <math>\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{-}(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A})</math>.
* [[Distributivity]] of multiplication by a scalar over addition: <math> c (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}) = c\mathbf{A}+c\mathbf{B}</math>. 
* Distributivity of scalar product over addition: <math>\left(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}\right)\cdot\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}+\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{C}</math>.
* Distributivity of vector product over addition: <math>(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{C}+\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}</math>.
* [[Scalar triple product]]: <math display="block">\mathbf{A}\cdot (\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{B}\cdot (\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{C}\cdot (\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}) = |\mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{C}|= \begin{vmatrix}
A_{x} & B_{x} & C_{x}\\
A_{y} & B_{y} & C_{y}\\
A_{z} & B_{z} & C_{z}\end{vmatrix}.</math>
* [[Vector triple product]]: <math>\mathbf{A}\times (\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}) = (\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C} )\mathbf{B}- (\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})\mathbf{C}</math>.
* [[Jacobi identity]]: <math display="block">\mathbf{A}\times (\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C} )+\mathbf{C}\times (\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B} )+ \mathbf{B}\times (\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{A} )= \mathbf 0 .</math>
* [[Lagrange's identity]]: <math>|\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}|^2  =   (\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{A}) (\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{B})-(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B})^2</math>.

===Quadruple product===
The name "quadruple product" is used for two different products,<ref>{{harvnb|Gibbs|Wilson|1901|loc=§42 of section "Direct and skew products of vectors", p.77 |year=1901}}</ref> the scalar-valued '''scalar quadruple product''' and the vector-valued '''vector quadruple product''' or '''vector product of four vectors'''.

==== Scalar quadruple product ====
The '''scalar quadruple product'''  is defined as the [[dot product]] of two [[cross product]]s:
:<math> (\mathbf{a \times b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d}) \ ,</math>
where '''a, b, c, d''' are vectors in three-dimensional Euclidean space.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{harvnb|Gibbs|Wilson|1901|p=76}}</ref> It can be evaluated using the [[Binet-Cauchy identity]]:<ref name=autogenerated1 />
:<math> (\mathbf{a \times b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d}) = (\mathbf{a \cdot c})(\mathbf{b \cdot d}) - (\mathbf{a \cdot d})(\mathbf{b \cdot c}) \ . </math>
or using the [[determinant]]:
:<math>(\mathbf{a \times b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d}) =\begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{a\cdot c} & \mathbf{a\cdot d} \\
 \mathbf{b\cdot c} & \mathbf{b\cdot d}  \end{vmatrix} \ . </math>

====Vector quadruple product ====
The '''vector quadruple product'''  is defined as the [[cross product]] of two cross products:
:<math> (\mathbf{a \times b}) \mathbf{\times} (\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d}) \ ,</math>
where '''a, b, c, d''' are vectors in three-dimensional Euclidean space.<ref name=autogenerated2>{{harvnb|Gibbs|Wilson|1901|pp=77 ''ff''}}</ref> It can be evaluated using the identity:<ref>{{harvnb|Gibbs|Wilson|1901|p=77}}</ref>
:<math> (\mathbf{a \times b} )\mathbf{\times} (\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d}) = (\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{d})) \mathbf c - (\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})) \mathbf d \ .</math>

Equivalent forms can be obtained using the identity:<ref>{{harvnb|Gibbs|Wilson|1901|loc=Equation 27, p. 77}}</ref><ref name="Soni">{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-3H5V0LGBOgC&pg=PA11|title=Mechanics and relativity|author=Vidwan Singh Soni| publisher=PHI Learning Pvt. Ltd.| year=2009 | isbn=978-81-203-3713-8| pages=11–12| chapter=§1.10.2 Vector quadruple product}}</ref><ref name="Gibbs">This formula is applied to spherical trigonometry by {{cite book| url=https://archive.org/details/vectoranalysisa00wilsgoog|title=Vector analysis: a text-book for the use of students of mathematics|author=Edwin Bidwell Wilson, Josiah Willard Gibbs| publisher=Scribner|year=1901|pages=[https://archive.org/details/vectoranalysisa00wilsgoog/page/n101 77]''ff''|chapter=§42 in ''Direct and skew products of vectors''}}</ref>
:<math>(\mathbf{b} \cdot (\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}))\mathbf a - (\mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{d} \times \mathbf{a}))\mathbf b+(\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}))\mathbf{c} -(\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}))\mathbf d = 0 \ . </math>

This identity can also be written using [[tensor]] notation and the [[Einstein summation]] convention as follows:
:<math>(\mathbf{a \times b} )\mathbf{\times} (\mathbf{c}\times \mathbf{d})=\varepsilon_{ijk} a^i c^j d^k b^l - \varepsilon_{ijk} b^i c^j d^k a^l=\varepsilon_{ijk} a^i b^j d^k c^l - \varepsilon_{ijk} a^i b^j c^k d^l</math>
where {{math|''ε<sub>ijk</sub>''}} is the [[Levi-Civita symbol]].

Related relationships:
* A consequence of the previous equation:<ref>{{Cite web|title=linear algebra - Cross-product identity| url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3496791/cross-product-identity| access-date=2021-10-07|website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref> <math display="block">|\mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{C}|\,\mathbf{D}= (\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{D} )\left(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}\right)+\left(\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{D}\right)\left(\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{A}\right)+\left(\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{D}\right)\left(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\right).</math>
*In 3 dimensions, a vector '''D''' can be expressed in terms of [[basis vectors]] {'''A''','''B''','''C'''} as:<ref name="Coffin">{{cite book |title=Vector analysis: an introduction to vector-methods and their various applications to physics and mathematics |author=Joseph George Coffin |url=https://archive.org/details/vectoranalysisa00coffgoog |page=[https://archive.org/details/vectoranalysisa00coffgoog/page/n84 56] |year=1911 |publisher=Wiley |edition=2nd}}</ref><math display="block">\mathbf D \ =\ \frac{\mathbf{D} \cdot (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C})}{|\mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{C}|}\ \mathbf A +\frac{\mathbf{D} \cdot (\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{A})}{|\mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{B}\, \mathbf{C}|}\ \mathbf B + \frac{\mathbf{D} \cdot (\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B})}{|\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{B}\, \mathbf{C}|}\ \mathbf C.</math>

== Applications==
These relations are useful for deriving various formulas in spherical and Euclidean geometry. For example, if four points are chosen on the unit sphere, ''A, B, C, D'', and unit vectors drawn from the center of the sphere to the four points, '''a, b, c, d''' respectively, the identity:
:<math>(\mathbf{a \times b})\mathbf{\cdot}(\mathbf{c \times d}) = (\mathbf {a\cdot c })(\mathbf {b\cdot d })-(\mathbf{ a\cdot d })(\mathbf {b\cdot c }) \ , </math>
in conjunction with the relation for the magnitude of the cross product:
:<math>\|\mathbf{a \times b}\| = a b \sin \theta_{ab} \ , </math>
and the dot product:
:<math>\mathbf{a \cdot b} = a b \cos \theta_{ab} \ , </math>
where ''a = b'' = 1 for the unit sphere, results in the identity among the angles attributed to Gauss:
:<math>\sin \theta_{ab}\sin \theta_{cd}\cos x = \cos\theta_{ac}\cos\theta_{bd} - \cos\theta_{ad} \cos \theta_{bc} \ , </math>
where ''x'' is the angle between '''a''' × '''b''' and '''c''' × '''d''', or equivalently, between the planes defined by these vectors.<ref name=autogenerated2 />
